rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lawful exceptions to the prohibition on killing include the cases named in 9:5, including a previously married adulterer, retaliation for murder, and apostasy with departure from the community.
rows.anchor: لا يحل دم امرىء مسلم إلا بإحدى ثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet instructed that when allegiance is given to two caliphs, the later claimant should be killed.
rows.anchor: إذا بويع لخليفتين فاقتلوا الآخر منهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet ordered killing both the active and passive partners in male same-sex intercourse; Qurtubi says fuller treatment will come in al-Aʿraf.
rows.anchor: من وجدتموه يعمل عمل قوم لوط فاقتلوا الفاعل والمفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception also covers the prescribed punishment for those who wage war against God and spread corruption on earth.
rows.anchor: إنما جزآء الذين يحاربون الله ورسوله ويسعون في الأرض فسادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The legal treatment of armed conflict among believers is also relevant to the qualification that killing must be justified.
rows.anchor: وإن طآئفتان من المؤمنين اقتتلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who breaks Muslim unity, defies the community's imam, loots families and property, rebels against authority, and refuses its judgment is to be killed as a corrupter; this explains “except by right.”
rows.anchor: من شق عصا المسلمين وخالف إمام جماعتهم وفرق كلمتهم وسعى في الأرض فسادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet said believers have equal standing in blood, even the least of them can give protection, a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever, a protected non-Muslim is not killed while under protection, and people of different religions do not inherit one another.
rows.anchor: المؤمنون تتكافأ دماؤهم ويسعى بذمتهم أدناهم لا يقتل مسلم بكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Bakra reports the Prophet warning that someone who unjustly kills a protected non-Muslim is barred from Paradise; one version says its scent can be found from seventy years away.
rows.anchor: من قتل معاهدا في غير كنهه حرم الله عليه الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A version in Abu Dawud says the killer of a protected person will not smell Paradise, whose scent reaches from seventy years away; Bukhari's version from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr says forty years.
rows.anchor: من قتل رجلا من أهل الذمة لم يجد ريح الجنة وإن ريحها ليوجد من مسيرة سبعين عاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” points to the prohibitions just listed; the attached address pronouns are vocative and have no grammatical case, while “enjoined” means a decisive, actionable command and its subject pronoun refers to God.
rows.anchor: هذه المحرمات. والكاف والميم للخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matar al-Warraq transmits through Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar that ʿUthman addressed his companions, asking why they were killing him and saying he had heard the Prophet state the rule on lawful Muslim blood.
rows.anchor: عن نافع عن ابن عمر أن عثمان بن عفان رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the continuation of the report, ʿUthman swears he neither committed adultery, killed anyone liable to retaliation, nor apostatized, and affirms his faith; he says these were the matters God enjoined so people might understand.
rows.anchor: فوالله ما زنيت في جاهلية ولا إسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Approach an orphan's property only in the way best for the orphan, by protecting its principal and growing its returns; Qurtubi prefers this as the most comprehensive interpretation.
rows.anchor: وهذا أحسن الأقوال في هذا فإنه جامع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the permitted approach as trading with the orphan's property, while forbidding buying from or borrowing it.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: { ولا تقربوا مال اليتيم إلا بالتي هي أحسن }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An orphan's “maturity” requires both bodily strength and experiential understanding; the unrestricted wording is clarified by 4:6, which joins reaching marriageable age with sound judgment.
rows.anchor: وقد تكون في المعرفة بالتجربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If an orphan receives property after physical maturity but before sound judgment, he may squander it on desires and be left destitute.
rows.anchor: فلو مكن اليتيم من ماله قبل حصول المعرفة وبعد حصول القوة لأذهبه في شهواته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan is singled out because people neglect him and his father is absent; attending to one who has lost a father merits special care, and God is the orphan's adversary against an abuser.
rows.anchor: وخص اليتيم بهذا الشرط لغفلة الناس عنه وافتقاد الآباء لأبنائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even after reaching maturity, an orphan's property may only be approached in the best way; the verse implies that once maturity and sound judgment are seen, his property is to be handed over.
rows.anchor: وليس بلوغ الأشد يبيح قرب ماله بغير الأحسن لأن الحرمة في حق البالغ ثابتة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the orphan's “maturity” with reaching puberty.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن زيد: بلوغه وقال أهل المدينة.

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: The people of Medina require both puberty and evidence of sound judgment for an orphan's maturity.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المدينة. بلوغه وإيناس رشده

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa sets the orphan's age of maturity at twenty-five.
rows.anchor: وعند أبي حنيفة: خمس وعشرون سنة.

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi objects that Abu Hanifa disallows establishing fixed measures by analogy or reasoning yet fixes this age using weak reports; he sharply contrasts Abu Hanifa's surroundings with Malik's scholarly environment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وعجبا من أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the age of full strength culminates at the end of mature adulthood, citing Suhaym ibn Wathil's line about a man of fifty whose strength is gathered.
rows.anchor: أخو خمسين مجتمع أشدي ونجذني مداورة الشؤون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ashudd” has no singular in one account, like “al-ānuk” (lead); alternatives give “shadd” or “shiddah,” and lexical authorities disagree over whether these are attested forms or only analogy.
rows.anchor: والأشد واحد لا جمع له بمنزلة الآنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is connected with the rising intensity of daytime, as in “the height of the day”; Muhammad al-Dabbi recited ʿAntara's line as evidence for “shadd al-nahar.”
rows.anchor: وأصله من شد النهار أي ارتفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second poet's line uses “shadd al-nahar” for the time when a woman passes by; it is another usage supporting the expression.
rows.anchor: وكان محمد بن محمد الضبي ينشد بيت عنترة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh says the singular is “shiddah”; al-Jawhari finds this semantically apt but notes that the plural pattern does not normally pluralize a faʿlah noun as afʿul.
rows.anchor: وكان سيبويه يقول: واحده شدة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms such as “shadd” for “ashudd” are analogical rather than heard from Arabic usage, like the proposed singular “ibul” for “ababil”; Abu Zayd also records “shadā” for hardship and “ashadda” for possessing a strong riding animal.
rows.anchor: وليس هو شيئا سمع من العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulfilling measure and weight justly means giving and receiving accurately in sales; “qist” means justice.
rows.anchor: أي بالاعتدال في الأخذ والعطاء عند البيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The capacity qualification excuses unavoidable variations between measures, since people are accountable only for care and precision within human control.
rows.anchor: وهذا يقتضي أن هذه الأوامر إنما هي فيما يقع تحت قدرة البشر من التحفظ والتحرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take “measure” to mean the measuring vessel itself, which explains its pairing with the scale.
rows.anchor: ولهذا عطف عليه بالميزان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars say the seller is required to give exactly what is owed, not extra, and the creditor to accept exactly what is owed, not less, so neither is burdened with resentment.
rows.anchor: أمر المعطي بإيفاء رب الحق حقه الذي هو له

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: A report reaching Ibn ʿAbbas says public embezzlement brings fear, widespread adultery death, short measure and weight loss of provision, unjust rule bloodshed, and treachery in covenants an enemy's domination.
rows.anchor: ما ظهر الغلول في قوم قط إلا ألقى الله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas warns non-Arabs that the two practices which ruined earlier peoples were measure and weight.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا: إنكم معشر الأعاجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to speak justly covers legal judgments and testimony, even where the truth goes against relatives.
rows.anchor: ولو كان الحق على مثل قراباتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulfilling God's covenant is general for all obligations He gave His servants; it may also include agreements between people, called God's covenant because He commands that they be kept.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يراد به جميع ما انعقد بين إنسانين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This great verse links to the preceding commands: after prohibitions and orders, it warns against every other path and orders following God's path.
rows.anchor: فإنه لما نهى وأمر حذر هنا عن اتباع غير سبيله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ and al-Kisaʾi parse “wa-an” with an implied “I recite”; al-Farraʾ also allows genitive coordination, while al-Khalil and Sibawayh understand “and because this is My path,” citing 72:18.
rows.anchor: أي وأتل أن هذا صراطي عن الفراء والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi read “wa-inna” with a kasra as a new sentence: what has just been mentioned is God's straight path.
rows.anchor: على الاستئناف أي الذي ذكر في هذه الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yaʿqub read the conjunction in its light form; it behaves like the heavy form with an implicit pronoun of the story, may be nominative or accusative, or may be emphatic and extra, as in 12:96.
rows.anchor: إلا أن فيه ضمير القصة والشان أي وأنه هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is Islam, the Prophet Muhammad's revealed law, and its end is Paradise; following the main road saves, while branching paths lead to Hell, and the phrase about paths means they cause deviation.
rows.anchor: الطريق الذي هو دين الإسلام

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: In a soundly authenticated report in al-Darimi, Ibn Masʿud says the Prophet drew one line as God's path and side lines as other paths, each with a devil calling people to it, then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مسعود قال:

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir reports in Ibn Majah a similar lesson: the Prophet drew the center line as God's path, added lines to the right and left, and recited the verse.
rows.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله قال:

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the divergent paths include Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, other religions, religious innovations, deviant legal doctrines, and excessive disputation or speculative theology; Qurtubi agrees this is correct.
rows.anchor: ومظنة لسوء المعتقد قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: A report cited from al-Tabari pictures the straight path as beginning near the Prophet and ending in Paradise, with side roads that lead to Hell when callers draw people onto them.
rows.anchor: قال لابن مسعود: ما الصراط المستقيم؟ قال:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud urges learning before knowledge disappears with its bearers, warns against hair-splitting, excess, and innovations, and calls people to the ancient way; al-Darimi transmits it.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن مسعود: تعلموا

rows.speaker: ابن شهاب
rows.claim: Ibn Shihab connects the warning against divergent paths to the warning that people split their religion into sects in 6:159.
rows.anchor: قال ابن شهاب: وهذا كقوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi urges holding firmly to the straight path and the sound Sunnah followed by the early righteous generations as the route to safety and gain.
rows.anchor: والتمسك بالطريق المستقيم والسنن القويم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet's instruction: take what he commands and stop what he forbids.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: العرباض بن سارية
rows.claim: In a report al-Tirmidhi authenticates in meaning, the Prophet's tearful farewell counsel says his community has a clear way, will face much disagreement, and must cling to his Sunnah and the rightly guided caliphs, reject innovations as misguidance, and obey even an Abyssinian slave.
rows.anchor: عن العرباض بن سارية قال:

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: In a letter about predestination, Umar counsels piety, moderation, the Prophetic Sunnah, abandoning innovations, and staying with the community; he says the first generations had sufficient knowledge and insight, while later people either fell short or went beyond them.
rows.anchor: فكتب إليه: أما بعد، فإني أوصيك

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله التستري
rows.claim: Sahl al-Tustari urges following transmitted precedent and the Sunnah, warning that soon those who mention the Prophet and imitate him in every state will be censured, shunned, disowned, and humiliated.
rows.anchor: قال سهل بن عبد الله التستري: عليكم بالاقتداء

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله التستري
rows.claim: Sahl says innovations spread because Sunnis debated their proponents publicly; had the innovators been left alone, their ideas would have died with them. He adds that Iblis first inspires devotional practice, then innovation, and strips the devotion away when it is proclaimed.
rows.anchor: قال سهل: إنما ظهرت البدعة على يدي أهل السنة

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl cites a report he calls the strongest about innovators: God bars an innovator from Paradise, so Jews and Christians are more hopeful than such a person.
rows.anchor: فاليهودي والنصراني أرجى منهم. قال سهل:

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl advises one who wants to honor his religion not to visit rulers, be alone with women, or argue with people of sectarian desires; he says to follow rather than innovate because enough has already been provided.
rows.anchor: قال سهل: من أراد أن يكرم دينه فلا يدخل على السلطان

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Darimi reports that Ibn Masʿud rejected a group counting repeated formulae of remembrance with pebbles in circles, telling them to count sins instead; he warned that good intentions do not guarantee a good act and called their practice an opening to misguidance.
rows.anchor: إلى عبد الله بن مسعود فقال: يا أبا عبد الرحمن

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: Asked about sectarian innovators, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz tells a man to hold to the religion of the Bedouins and the child at school, leaving other paths aside.
rows.anchor: وعن عمر بن عبد العزيز وسأله

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Awzaʿi recounts Iblis asking his followers how they reach Adam's children; they say through every route but repentance, so he vows to spread sectarian desires that people will not seek forgiveness for.
rows.anchor: وقال الأوزاعي: قال إبليس لأوليائه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says he does not know which is the greater blessing: being guided to Islam or being protected from sectarian desires.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ولا أدري أي النعمتين

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi explains that the people of desires are so called because they plunge into the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: إنما سموا أصحاب الأهواء

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Sahl rules against praying behind, marrying, or marrying into the Muʿtazila, calling them unbelievers for denying created Paradise and Hell, the bridge, intercession, punishment and angels of the grave, vision of God, and other doctrines while anathematizing believers.
rows.anchor: وسئل سهل بن عبد الله عن الصلاة خلف المعتزلة

rows.speaker: الفضيل بن عياض
rows.claim: Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad says that loving an innovator nullifies one's deeds and removes Islam's light from the heart; Qurtubi notes that he cited this earlier with more detail.
rows.anchor: وقال الفضيل بن عياض: من أحب صاحب بدعة

rows.speaker: سفيان الثوري
rows.claim: Sufyan al-Thawri says innovation is dearer to Iblis than sin because sin can be repented from whereas innovation is not repented from.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان الثوري: البدعة أحب إلى إبليس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls it worship to look at a Sunnah-following person who invites others to the Sunnah and forbids innovations.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: النظر إلى الرجل من أهل السنة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya urges adherence to the original practice before people split; Hasan al-Basri, hearing this from ʿAsim al-Ahwal, affirms that it is sincere and true advice.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: عليكم بالأمر الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi notes that the warning about Israel's seventy-two sects and this community's seventy-three was discussed earlier in Aal ʿImran.
rows.anchor: وقد مضى في «آل عمران» معنى قوله عليه السلام:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some learned authorities say the extra sect in Muhammad's community consists of people who oppose scholars and hate jurists, something unknown among earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: قال بعض العلماء العارفين: هذه الفرقة التي زادت

rows.speaker: رافع بن خديج
rows.claim: Rafiʿ ibn Khadij reports the Prophet warning of people who unknowingly deny God and the Quran by accepting part and rejecting part, making Iblis equal to God in creation, power, and provision, and provoking enmity and argument; he calls them the community's heretics.
rows.anchor: روى رافع بن خديج أنه سمع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi links the ban on following divergent paths to the prohibition on sitting with people who dispute God's signs, citing 6:68; 4:140 later says those who sit with them share their ruling.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة النهي عن مجالسة أهل البدع والأهواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group of imams, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Awzaʿi, and Ibn al-Mubarak, say a persistent companion of innovators is treated as one of them; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz applied the same principle to people sitting with wine drinkers.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب إلى هذا جماعة من أئمة هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When told he merely sat with innovators to dispute them, the response was that he must stop, and if he refuses he is joined to them in judgment.
rows.anchor: قيل له: فإنه يقول إني أجالسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A polytheist among those Muslims were ordered to fight who asks for protection should receive it so that he can hear and understand the Quran's rulings; if he accepts, well, otherwise he must be escorted to safety. Qurtubi says there is no disagreement on this.
rows.anchor: أي من الذين أمرتك بقتالهم.

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: If an enemy combatant encountered on a road in Muslim territory asks for protection, Malik considers the situation ambiguous and says to return him to safety.
rows.anchor: قال مالك: إذا وجد الحربي

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qasim gives the same ruling for a trader who lands on the coast, believing traders could sell without being attacked: return him to safety.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن القاسم: وكذلك الذي يوجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's apparent case is protection for someone who wishes to hear the Quran and consider Islam; granting protection for other purposes is instead justified by Muslim interests.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية إنما هي فيمن يريد سماع القرآن والنظر في الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All scholars accept the ruler's grant of protection because he represents the public interest and acts for all in securing benefits and repelling harms.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف بين كافة العلماء أن أمان السلطان جائز لأنه مقدم للنظر والمصلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All scholars accept a free man's protection pledge, though Ibn Habib says the imam should review it.
rows.anchor: فالحر يمضي أمانه عند كافة العلماء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known Maliki, Shafiʿi, Hanbali, and other juristic position permits a slave to give protection; Abu Hanifa and a second Maliki opinion reject it. Qurtubi prefers permission based on the hadith that even the lowest Muslim can guarantee protection, and says a free woman is still more entitled; lack of a war stipend is irrelevant.
rows.anchor: وأما العبد فله الأمان في مشهور المذهب وبه قال الشافعي وأصحابه وأحمد

rows.speaker: عبد الملك بن الماجشون
rows.claim: Ibn al-Majishun says a woman's protection is not effective unless the imam approves it, an isolated position against the majority.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الملك بن الماجشون: لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A minor who is capable of fighting may give protection because he belongs to the fighting force and its defending unit.
rows.anchor: وأما الصبي فإذا أطاق القتال جاز أمانه لأنه من جملة المقاتلة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi hold that this verse was abrogated by the order to fight the polytheists.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب الضحاك والسدي إلى أن هذه الآية منسوخة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and Mujahid say the verse remains operative until the end of time; Qurtubi endorses this as correct, citing ʿAli's refusal to kill a man seeking to hear God's word after the four-month period.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هي محكمة سنة إلى يوم القيامة وقاله مجاهد.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr recounts a polytheist asking ʿAli whether someone could visit Muhammad to hear God's word after the four-month grace period; ʿAli answers no one may kill him because this verse commands protection until he hears it.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: جاء رجل من المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi rejects the claim that the protection rule applied only during the four-month truce and concludes that the verse is still operative.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الصحيح. والآية محكمة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “in ahad,” “ahad” is nominative with an implied verb; this is acceptable after conditional “in” but improper with its sister particles, which Sibawayh distinguishes because “in” is specific to conditions.
rows.anchor: «أحد» مرفوع بإضمار فعل كالذي بعده.

rows.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Yazid rejects Sibawayh's claim that “in” does not occur outside conditionals: it can mean “ma” or be a light form of emphatic “inna,” but remains ambiguous unlike the other particles.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن يزيد: أما قوله: «لأنها لا تكون في غيره» فغلط

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh cites a line of poetry using conditional “in” to demonstrate its use in a conditional clause.
rows.anchor: وأنشد سيبويه: لا تجزعي إن منفسا أهلكته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars including Abu al-Hasan, al-Qadi Abu Bakr, al-Qalanisi, Ibn Mujahid, and al-Isfarayini infer that God's speech is heard when a reciter reads it, since the verse explicitly says “the speech of God” is heard.
rows.anchor: قاله الشيخ أبو الحسن والقاضي أبو بكر وأبو العباس القلانسي وابن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims say “we heard God's speech” when Quran is recited and distinguish it from recited poetry; Qurtubi recalls the doctrine that God's speech is neither letter nor sound.
rows.anchor: إجماع المسلمين على أن القارىء إذا قرأ فاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rebuts polytheists and establishes the proof: if they acknowledge God's acts, the case is clear; if not, any rational person must recognize that the heavens and earth have a creator, a truth close to immediate necessity.
rows.anchor: المراد بمساق هذا الكلام الرد على المشركين وتقرير الحجة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Provision from heaven is rain and provision from earth is vegetation.
rows.anchor: أي بالمطر. { والأرض } بالنبات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God owns hearing and sight because He made and created them for people.
rows.anchor: { أمن يملك السمع والأبصار } أي من جعلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples of bringing the living from the dead include vegetation from earth, a person from a sperm drop, an ear of grain from a seed, a bird from an egg, and a believer from a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: { ومن يخرج الحي من الميت } أي النبات من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Managing the affair means determining and carrying it out.
rows.anchor: { ومن يدبر الأمر } أي يقدره ويقضيه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists will answer “God,” since they believe He is the Creator; alternatively, an honest and thoughtful person will reach this answer.
rows.anchor: { فسيقولون الله } لأنهم كانوا يعتقدون أن الخالق هو الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding question urges them to fear God's punishment and retribution in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: أفلا تخافون عقابه ونقمته في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who does these acts is the true Lord, unlike the beings associated with Him; after leaving worship of the true deity, nothing remains but error.
rows.anchor: أي هذا الذي يفعل هذه الأشياء هو ربكم الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some earlier commentators read the verse as saying that everything after God is error, and restrict its subject to belief and unbelief rather than deeds.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المتقدمين: ظاهر هذه الآية يدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view defines unbelief as covering truth and calls anything other than truth error, with the unlawful error and the permissible guidance because God alone permits and forbids; Qurtubi prefers the first interpretation from the preceding argument about God's acts and exclusive right to worship.
rows.anchor: والصحيح الأول لأن قبل «قل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foundational issue of God's oneness has no intermediate status between truth and falsehood; this is unlike derivative legal questions, which concern rulings attached to established things.
rows.anchor: حكمت هذه الآية بأنه ليس بين الحق والباطل منزلة ثالثة في هذه المسألة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinction is illustrated by 5:48's different laws for communities and the hadith that lawful and unlawful are clear while doubtful matters lie between them; those examples concern practical rulings, not the oneness of God.
rows.anchor: لكل جعلنا منكم شرعة ومنهاجا

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports the Prophet's night prayer supplication praising God as the truth, calling His promise, word, meeting, Paradise, Hell, Hour, prophets, and Muhammad true.
rows.anchor: الثالثة ثبت عن عائشة رضي الله عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are the Truth” means the necessarily existent: God's own existence has no prior or subsequent nonexistence, whereas every other existent is preceded by nonexistence, may cease, and depends on a creator.
rows.anchor: أي الواجب الوجود وأصله من حق الشيء أي ثبت ووجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi calls Labid's line “everything except God is perishing” the truest poetic utterance and links it to 28:88, where everything perishes except God's face.
rows.anchor: ألا كل شيء ما خلا الله باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth and misguidance, like truth and falsehood, form the recognized linguistic and legal contrast; 31:30 says God is the Truth and what people invoke besides Him is falsehood.
rows.anchor: ذلك بأن الله هو الحق وأن ما يدعون من دونه الباطل

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArafa defines misguidance in Arabic as taking a route other than the straight course, or losing something.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عرفة: الضلالة عند العرب سلوك غير سبيل القصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Misguidance derives from straying from a road's direction and, in legal usage, is especially used for departure from sound belief rather than deeds.
rows.anchor: والضلال حقيقته الذهاب عن الحق أخذ من ضلال الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes take “He found you astray and guided you” as meaning unaware rather than disbelieving, because the Prophet lacked prior knowledge of scripture and faith.
rows.anchor: ووجدك ضآلا فهدى [الضحى: 7] أي غافلا، في أحد التأويلات

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik interprets “what after truth except error?” as condemning chess and backgammon.
rows.anchor: عن مالك في قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik disliked playing the game of fourteen with one's wife, saying it is not a believer's conduct and citing the verse.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك: ما يعجبني! وليس

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik calls chess bad, false, and one of the vain games, adding that a rational person should be deterred from such play by his beard and gray hair; al-Zuhri likewise calls it false and dislikes it.
rows.anchor: سئل يعني مالكا عن اللعب بالشطرنج فقال: لا خير فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among Malikis and most jurists, occasional secret chess without gambling at home is excused, but a habitual public player loses reputation and probity and has testimony rejected.
rows.anchor: أن من لم يقامر بها ولعب مع أهله في بيته مستترا به مرة في الشهر أو العام

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Shafiʿi's school does not reject the testimony of an otherwise upright chess or backgammon player absent foolishness, suspicion, or grave sin; gambling or being known for it does invalidate probity for consuming illicit wealth.
rows.anchor: وأما الشافعي فلا تسقط في مذهب أصحابه شهادة اللاعب بالنرد والشطرنج

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa's school regards chess, backgammon, the game of fourteen, and all amusements as disliked but accepts the testimony of a player whose good deeds outweigh faults if he commits no evident major sin.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: يكره اللعب بالشطرنج

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi reports the Shafiʿi distinction that chess exercises thought and ingenuity, whereas backgammon is chance-based gambling like divining with arrows.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: قالت الشافعية إن الشطرنج يخالف النرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The backgammon and chess pieces are described as made of boxwood and elephant bone; backgammon is also called al-batil, al-kaʿab, al-arn, and nardshir.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: النرد قطع مملوءة من خشب البقس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim transmits the Prophet's comparison of playing nardshir to dipping one's hand into pork and its blood; scholars explain this as preparing it to eat, which is forbidden.
rows.anchor: في صحيح مسلم عن سليمان بن بريدة عن أبيه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound hadith from Abu Musa says playing nard disobeys God and His Messenger; Qurtubi reads the prohibition generally, including chess and play without gambling, as the safer position, though one could limit it to gambling in light of early permissions.
rows.anchor: وهو حديث صحيح، وهو يحرم اللعب بالنرد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الحليمي
rows.claim: Al-Halimi cites a report that playing chess is disobedience to God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبد الله الحليمي في كتاب منهاج الدين:

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAli rebukes Banu Tamim players for wasting their purpose in life and says he would strike their faces with the pieces were it not that doing so might become customary.
rows.anchor: وعن علي رضي الله عنه أنه مر على مجلس من مجالس بني تميم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says chess is worse than backgammon.
rows.anchor: وسئل ابن عمر عن الشطرنج فقال: هي شر من النرد

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abu Musa al-Ashʿari says only a sinner plays chess.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو موسى الأشعري: لا يلعب بالشطرنج

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar dismisses chess as a Zoroastrian practice.
rows.anchor: وسئل أبو جعفر عن الشطرنج فقال: دعونا من هذه المجوسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long prophetic report says God despises players of backgammon, chess, walnuts, and dice, and those who watch them lose all good deeds; Qurtubi says these traditions support prohibition even without gambling and had discussed their pairing with wine in al-Maʾida.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآثار كلها تدل على تحريم اللعب بها بلا قمار

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi says some Shafiʿis went so far as to recommend chess, playing it in schools or mosques after study and attributing it to early Muslims; Qurtubi rejects these attributions and claims of sharpening intelligence.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي في قبسه: وقد جوزه الشافعي

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل عطاء المقدسي
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl ʿAtaʾ al-Maqdisi argues that chess teaches warfare; al-Turtushi replies that it spoils war strategy by telling the king to move out of the way when war aims to seize him.
rows.anchor: سمعت الإمام أبا الفضل عطاء المقدسي يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An account of ʿUmar describing chess as a model of war does not prove he permitted idle chess; he said only that a device useful for warfare would be unobjectionable, assuming it served military learning. Reports of companions not forbidding it may reflect the same assumption or lack of the later hadith.
rows.anchor: فقال: لا بأس بما كان من آلة الحرب

rows.speaker: الحليمي
rows.claim: Al-Halimi says that once an authenticated report is established, no one has an argument against it; it binds everyone.
rows.anchor: قال الحليمي: وإذا صح الخبر فلا حجة لأحد معه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar filled in the pits in a children's game called al-kajja and forbade the children from playing it.
rows.anchor: أن عبد الله بن عمر مر بغلمان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report cited by al-Harawi from Ibn ʿAbbas says gambling occurs in everything, even children playing al-kajja; Ibn al-Aʿrabi explains it as children rolling a rag into a ball and gambling with it.
rows.anchor: في حديث ابن عباس: في كل شيء قمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final question asks how people turn their reasoning toward worship of beings that neither provide, give life, nor cause death.
rows.anchor: أي كيف تصرفون عقولكم إلى عبادة ما لا يرزق ولا يحيي ولا يميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is a nominal sentence whose subject is “those” and predicate is “the ones who lost themselves”; what they fabricated has disappeared and been lost.
rows.anchor: ابتداء وخبر. { وضل عنهم ما كانوا يفترون }

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil and Sibawayh take “la jarama” as “certainly,” treating it as one indivisible expression; “anna” is nominative. Al-Farraʾ and Muhammad ibn Yazid also transmit this analysis.
rows.anchor: فقال الخليل وسيبويه: { لا جرم } بمعنى حق

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: A second interpretation from al-Khalil and al-Farraʾ makes “la jarama” mean “inevitably” or “without doubt.”
rows.anchor: وعن الخليل أيضا أن معناها لا بد ولا محالة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses “la” as denial of the claim that idols benefit, and “jarama” as “earned”: their deed earned loss, with the implied subject omitted and “anna” in the accusative; he supports the root with poetry.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: { لا } هاهنا نفي

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says “la jarama” means there is no restraint or prevention from their consequence.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: معنى { لا جرم } لا صد ولا منع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the expression as “no cutting can cut it off,” with the agent suppressed through frequent use; the root means cutting or stripping, as in harvesting dates, shearing wool, and taking meat from bones.
rows.anchor: فحذف الفاعل حين كثر استعماله والجرم القطع

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas reports four forms from al-Kisaʾi—“la jarama,” “wa-la ʿan dha jarama,” and “wa-la anna dha jarama” among them—and notes Fazarans' form without mīm; al-Farraʾ adds “la dha jarama” and a form with ḍamma on jīm.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وزعم الكسائي أن فيها أربع لغات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “At night” is a temporal circumstance; the brothers came after dark to make their excuse easier. A saying advises not seeking favors at night, when shame shows in the eyes, or trying to excuse a daytime wrong, when speech falters.
rows.anchor: أي ليلا، وهو ظرف يكون في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report tells that when Jacob heard them crying he asked what had happened and where Joseph was; they answered that they had raced off and the wolf ate him, after which he cried out and asked for the shirt.
rows.anchor: فروي أن يعقوب عليه السلام لما سمع بكاءهم قال:

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Ibn Hibban say Jacob collapsed unconscious at the claim that a wolf ate Joseph; Judah found no sign of life, lamented that they had lost their brother and killed their father, and Jacob woke at dawn with Reuben supporting him before Judah repeated their story.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وابن حبان: إنه لما قالوا

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb recounts Judah checking Jacob's breathing and pulse, then rebuking himself and his brothers for losing Joseph and nearly causing their father's death.
rows.anchor: قال وهب: ولقد وضع يهوذا يده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tears do not prove the truth of what someone says, since a person may manufacture tears, though some people can do this and others cannot.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: هذه الآية دليل على أن بكاء المرء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saying attributed to a sage says that mingled tears on cheeks reveal who is weeping and who is pretending.
rows.anchor: إذا اشتبكت دموع في خدود تبين من بكى ممن تباكى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nastabiq” is a derived form meaning “we race”; the alternative “nintadil” in ʿAbd Allah's reading means they engaged in archery, a type of competition.
rows.anchor: نفتعل، من المسابقة. وقيل: أي ننتضل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj calls archery a form of competition; al-Azhari distinguishes contests of arrows from horse races, with “competition” encompassing both.
rows.anchor: قاله الزجاج. وقال الأزهري: النضال في السهام

rows.speaker: أبو نصر القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri says the brothers might have been competing at archery, on horseback, or on foot; running trains the body for chasing an enemy and protecting sheep from a wolf.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري أبو نصر: «نستبق» أي في الرمي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Ibn Hibban understand that the brothers ran hard to see which of them was fastest.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وابن حبان: «نستبق»

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi calls racing a legitimate and excellent practice and aid to warfare; the Prophet raced on foot and with horses, and raced ʿAʾisha, first winning and later—when older—losing, then saying “this for that.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: المسابقة شرعة في الشريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi adds that Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ raced a man returning from Dhu Qarad to Medina and won; Muslim transmits it.
rows.anchor: قلت: وسابق سلمة بن الأكوع رجلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malik transmits that the Prophet raced trained horses from al-Hafya to Thaniyyat al-Wadaʿ and untrained horses from the latter place to the mosque of Banu Zurayq; Ibn ʿUmar joined the races.
rows.anchor: روى مالك عن نافع عن ابن عمر: أن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi derives three conditions from this sound report: the distance must be known, horses comparable in condition, and trained horses cannot race untrained horses over the same distance; the horses for this Sunnah are those prepared to fight enemies, not Muslims in civil strife.
rows.anchor: وهذا الحديث مع صحته في هذا الباب تضمن ثلاثة شروط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Muslim report from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr mentions travelers with the Prophet practicing archery during a stop.
rows.anchor: فمنا من يصلح خباءه، ومنا من ينتضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims agree that prize wagers are allowed only in archery, camels, and horses; al-Shafiʿi regards wagering in other contests as gambling.
rows.anchor: أجمع المسلمون على أن السبق لا يجوز على وجه الرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extra “or wing” in Abu al-Bakhtari's version of the hadith was fabricated for the caliph al-Rashid, so scholars rejected this narrator and his other fabrications.
rows.anchor: وقد زاد أبو البختري القاضي في حديث الخف والحافر والنصل

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik allows prizes only for horses and archery because they strengthen war effort, and prefers horse racing; the hadith's apparent scope also includes camels.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن مالك أنه قال: لا سبق إلا في الخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some jurists allow wagering only on horses, the customary Arab race; ʿAtaʾ reportedly allows it in any contest, but Qurtubi says such a general reading would license gambling, which is agreed to be forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقد منع بعض العلماء الرهان في كل شيء إلا في الخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Horse and camel races require a known finish and distance; archery also requires a known target, number of rounds, and agreed hit criterion such as piercing through or another specified strike.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز السبق في الخيل والإبل إلا في غاية معلومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first permitted prize arrangement is a ruler or other donor voluntarily offering a known award to the winner; the second is a one-sided stake, which the winner may take and the loser does not reclaim, with no scholarly disagreement.
rows.anchor: سبق يعطيه الوالي أو الرجل غير الوالي من ماله متطوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When both racers stake money for the winner, the arrangement is only permitted with a third entrant who could beat either: if the entrant wins, he takes both stakes; if either racer wins, that racer takes both, and the entrant neither pays nor receives.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه لا يجوز حتى يدخلا بينهما محللا لا يأمنا

rows.speaker: أبو علي بن خيران
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli ibn Khayran says the third, qualifying horse's racing ability must be unknown; he is called a muhallil because his participation makes the wager lawful.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي بن خيران من أصحاب الشافعي : وحكم الفرس المحلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars agree that when both racers stipulate that the winner takes the other's stake and there is no qualifying third entrant, the arrangement is gambling and forbidden.
rows.anchor: واتفق العلماء على أنه إن لم يكن بينهما محلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bukhari reports that the Prophet's she-camel al-ʿAdba was rarely beaten until a Bedouin's mount outran her; when Muslims were saddened, the Prophet said God lowers whatever worldly thing rises.
rows.anchor: وروى البخاري عن أنس قال: كان للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ناقة تسمى العضباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nasaʾi reports Abu Hurayra’s Prophetic hadith that a prize is permitted only for arrows, camel racing, or horse racing; jurists of the Hijaz and Iraq rely on it.
rows.anchor: لا سبق إلا في نصل أو خف أو حافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says a horse inserted between two is not gambling if its ability to beat them is uncertain, but is gambling if it is certain to lose; Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib similarly permits a horse wager with a qualifying entrant, as do al-Shafiʿi and most scholars.
rows.anchor: من أدخل فرسا بين فرسين وهو لا يأمن أن يسبق فليس بقمار

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik first said a qualifying entrant is unnecessary and did not follow Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, but later required one; Qurtubi calls Malik's latter view the better one.
rows.anchor: واختلف في ذلك قول مالك فقال مرة لا يجب المحلل

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar says only a horse's owner should ride it in a race; Qurtubi also says the rider should be an adult, though an owner riding is preferable.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه أنه قال: لا يركب الخيل

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi defines the minimum lead in racing as the muzzle or part of it passing, or the hindquarters or part; the same rule applies to archers, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan agrees.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي: وأقل السبق أن يسبق بالهادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet raced Abu Bakr and ʿUmar, winning himself while Abu Bakr came second and ʿUmar third; “Abu Bakr came second” means his horse's head reached the rear of the Prophet's horse.
rows.anchor: روي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه سابق أبا بكر وعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers left Joseph guarding their clothes, baggage, and belongings.
rows.anchor: أي عند ثيابنا وأقمشتنا حارسا لها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They reused Jacob's expressed fear that a wolf might eat Joseph as the basis for their lie.
rows.anchor: لما سمعوا أباهم يقول: «وأخاف أن يأكله الذئب»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “believe us” means “believe what we say.”
rows.anchor: { ومآ أنت بمؤمن لنا } أي بمصدق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their father did not believe them because their accusation was strong and evidence contradicted it.
rows.anchor: ولم يصدقهم يعقوب لما ظهر له منهم من قوة التهمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad and Ibn Ishaq take “wa-law kunna” to mean “even if we were” or “even though we were.”
rows.anchor: أي وإن كنا قاله المبرد وابن إسحق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, and others offer another interpretation: the brothers thought Jacob would doubt them even if they had been known as trustworthy, because of his intense love for Joseph.
rows.anchor: لشدة محبتك في يوسف قال معناه الطبري والزجاج وغيرهما.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the forged blood was from a slaughtered sheep or young goat; Qatada says it was from a gazelle.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: كان دم سخلة أو جدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kazib” describes the blood as a verbal noun meaning falsified or lied-about blood, like calling the inhabitants “the village” or using a verbal noun for the agent or object.
rows.anchor: أي جاءوا على قميصه بدم مكذوب فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and ʿAʾisha read “kadib” with dāl, meaning fresh blood; al-Shaʿbi also says it can mean changed blood, and the word may refer to the white mark on a youth's fingernail, like the contrasting colors on the shirt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعائشة: «بدم كدب»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God paired the brothers' blood-stained-shirt sign with a contrary sign: a wolf could not have eaten Joseph while leaving the shirt un-torn; Jacob noticed no hole or trace and inferred their lie.
rows.anchor: قرن الله بهذه العلامة علامة تعارضها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Jacob said the wolf would have torn the shirt if it had eaten Joseph; one transmission says the blood came from a young goat.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: كان الدم دم سخلة.

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi says the shirt bears three signs, but Qurtubi rejects this because the bloodied, torn, and later healing shirts are different garments; one alternative identifies the torn shirt with the one brought by the herald.
rows.anchor: وحكى الماوردي أن في القميص ثلاث آيات:

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: A report from al-Hasan says the brothers also claimed robbers had killed Joseph; their changing explanation increased Jacob's suspicion, since robbers would have taken the shirt and a wolf would have torn it.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم قالوا له: بل اللصوص قتلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists use the episode to support circumstantial evidence in cases such as sworn group liability: Jacob inferred the lie from the intact shirt, and judges should assess competing signs and rule according to the stronger indication; Ibn al-ʿArabi says there is no disagreement in acting on such evidence.
rows.anchor: استدل الفقهاء بهذه الآية في إعمال الأمارات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extended, unsourced narrative says Jacob asked for some trace of Joseph; the brothers showed his bloodied but un-torn shirt, leading Jacob to accuse them. They plotted to kill him, but Judah stopped them; they then brought a wolf tied and bloodied, which God enabled to speak and deny eating Joseph, saying he was a stranger searching for his own missing brother. Jacob released it and declared the brothers had proved their own guilt.
rows.anchor: روي أن يعقوب لما قالوا له: «فأكله الذئب» قال لهم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sawwalt” means embellished or made attractive: their souls had decorated some affair other than the one they described.
rows.anchor: أي زينت. { لكم أنفسكم أمرا }

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj understands “fa-sabrun jamil” as saying that Jacob's own state and belief would be beautiful patience.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: أي فشأني والذي أعتقده

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub takes the phrase to mean “my patience is beautiful patience.”
rows.anchor: وقال قطرب: أي فصبري صبر جميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says beautiful patience is what is better for Jacob, with an omitted predicate after the subject.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي فصبر جميل أولى بي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet defined beautiful patience as patience without complaint; Qurtubi says fuller discussion will appear at the end of the sura.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل عن الصبر الجميل فقال:

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim says ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read “fa-sabran jamilan” in the accusative, as did al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli and the codices of Anas and Abu Salih.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم: قرأ عيسى بن عمر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad prefers the nominative “fa-sabrun jamil” because it means “My Lord, I have beautiful patience”; the accusative is an absolute object meaning “I will surely be patient.” A poem illustrates the latter construction.
rows.anchor: المبرد: «فصبر جميل» بالرفع أولى من النصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beautiful patience has no distress or complaint; another interpretation says Jacob did not treat his sons with a gloomy face but continued to interact normally, indicating that he forgave them.
rows.anchor: والصبر الجميل هو الذي لا جزع فيه ولا شكوى

rows.speaker: حبيب بن أبي ثابت
rows.claim: Habib ibn Abi Thabit recounts that Jacob's eyebrows fell over his eyes from long years and grief; when God asked if he was complaining of Him, Jacob confessed a sin and asked forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وعن حبيب بن أبي ثابت أن يعقوب كان قد سقط حاجباه على عينيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God is the one whose help is sought” is a nominal sentence, subject and predicate; Jacob seeks help in bearing what his sons falsely describe.
rows.anchor: ابتداء وخبر. { على ما تصفون }

rows.speaker: ابن أبي رفاعة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Rifaʿa advises prudent people to question their own judgment: Jacob correctly suspected his sons' account of Joseph's disappearance, but later failed to do so when they said Benjamin had stolen and repeated that their souls had embellished an affair.
rows.anchor: قال ابن أبي رفاعة: ينبغي لأهل الرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God originated the heavens and earth without any earlier model; He sends water from clouds and produces fruit from trees as provision.
rows.anchor: أي أبدعها واخترعها على غير مثال سبق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made ships run at His command and subjected fresh rivers for drinking, irrigation, and cultivation, and salty seas for the different benefits they provide.
rows.anchor: يعني البحار العذبة لتشربوا منها وتسقوا وتزرعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon continually serve functions such as fostering plant growth; “dāʾibayn” means continuous work by established custom, or, in another view, uninterrupted orbit in obedience to God until the Resurrection, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.
rows.anchor: أي في إصلاح ما يصلحانه من النبات وغيره، والدؤوب مرور الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is for rest and day for seeking God's bounty, as also stated in 28:73.
rows.anchor: أي لتسكنوا في الليل، ولتبتغوا من فضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of “He gave you of all you asked” means He granted something from everything requested, with an ellipsis according to al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: أي أعطاكم من كل مسؤول سألتموه شيئا فحذف عن الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says God gave what people asked for and also what they never asked for—such as the sun, moon, and many blessings He initiated; a third regards “min” as extra and reads that He gave everything requested.
rows.anchor: ومن كل ما لم تسألوه فحذف، فلم نسأله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and others read “wa-atākum min kulli” with a tanwin on “kull”; this reading is reported also from Hasan and Qatada and is interpreted negatively, as referring to what was not asked for, such as sun and moon. Another parsing takes “ma” as a relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس والضحاك وغيرهما { وءاتكم من كل }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessings of God are too numerous to count or encompass, including hearing, sight, the shaping of bodies, health, and provision.
rows.anchor: { لا تحصوها } ولا تطيقوا عدها، ولا تقوموا بحصرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since these blessings come from God, people should not exchange them for disbelief but should use them to obey Him.
rows.anchor: وهذه النعم من الله، فلم تبدلون نعمة الله بالكفر؟

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the human as Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أراد أبا جهل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes “the human” as the generic category but intends all disbelievers.
rows.anchor: أبا جهل. وقيل: جميع الكفار.
